content: It must be simple enough to fulfill surveillance requirements. It should allow the collection of multiple reports for individual cases. The system must support de-duplication of data. Both automated and manual data quality checks should be incorporated. The system should be capable of accepting, cleaning, storing, and exporting data for analysis. It must facilitate data transfer between subnational and national levels. Compliance with national laws governing public health data handling is essential. Data collected at sites should align with the case report forms used in public health facilities, particularly in countries where most HIV testing and care occur in such facilities using standardized data collection tools. Interoperability for electronic uploads should be included. The system should adhere to established data standards and include a data dictionary. Development and management of the system should be handled by skilled individuals or commercial suppliers. Surveillance policies, processes, and data systems must comply with national or international standards to protect patient privacy and data security. Confidentiality and security considerations should be integrated into every step of the system design. For instance, secure methods must be developed to transport case reports from facilities to the surveillance program. The surveillance system should be designed to maximize the likelihood of achieving recommended performance standards. Active surveillance conducted by designated personnel has been shown to improve the completeness, timeliness, and accuracy of case surveillance. Laboratory reporting enhances the completeness of case ascertainment and provides critical laboratory variables. Human and financial resources must also be considered when designing or upgrading the system. For example, there may be only one epidemiologist responsible for all disease notification systems at a subnational level. A surveillance system should include personnel capable of performing the following functions: Directing and coordinating national surveillance activities. Conducting national epidemiological analyses. Developing and enforcing confidentiality, security, and system protections. Managing national and subnational surveillance data. Supervising and conducting facility-level reporting. Managing both paper-based and electronic data at the facility level. Reviewing facility-level reports for data and clinical quality improvement. National regulations, laws, policies, and procedures for HIV case surveillance should be documented in an official technical guidance document, which serves as a reference tool for all individuals involved in surveillance activities. This document, also known as an operations manual, should be available at both national and subnational levels and include components such as a glossary of terms, surveillance case definitions, reporting pathways, data transmission procedures, and security and confidentiality requirements. Pilot testing may be necessary in countries where implementation methods are not well-defined. This allows for system modifications before a national rollout. The pilot phase can inform the human and financial resources required for implementing and sustaining HIV case surveillance. Once the system design is complete, plans for national rollout should be developed, either in phases or with a single start date. All staff involved in surveillance activities must be trained, and technical guidance documents and necessary supplies (e.g., case report forms) should be distributed. Enhanced and frequent monitoring is recommended until the system is well-established and performance standards are met. Ongoing training for new staff and feedback to surveillance and facility staff are essential. Data analysis and dissemination should occur as early as possible, considering reporting delays and allowing adequate time for complete reporting. Historical data collection may be challenging in some countries. For newly diagnosed individuals or those reaching a new sentinel event, case reports will be submitted. However, for stable individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) without routine viral load monitoring, decisions must be made on how to obtain reports for these cases. Short-term staff may need to be hired to collect historical case reports. HIV case surveillance data can describe the epidemic in terms of people, place, and time, and detect outbreaks or clusters of infection. It can also provide insights into the characteristics of newly diagnosed individuals, those with advanced HIV disease, and, in settings with reliable mortality data, individuals who have died. Surveillance data can be used to strengthen prevention and treatment activities in areas with high diagnosis rates and to identify where the epidemic is concentrated. Data from surveillance systems can be combined with other information, such as program monitoring, qualitative studies, vital statistics, and surveys, to account for changes in the epidemic. Analytical techniques like triangulation and data synthesis can correlate surveillance data with other sources. Surveillance systems that compile HIV care cascade indicators provide opportunities to investigate and address gaps in the care cascade. Surveillance data should be analyzed and presented in formats suitable for the target audience, such as annual reports, epidemic reports, data fact sheets, and presentations. Automated data analysis processes should be developed for future use. Incomplete case ascertainment limits data representativeness and diminishes the utility of HIV case reporting as a surveillance tool. Data analysis should account for reporting delays and be conducted by staff familiar with the data and its limitations. Data should be presented in a way that preserves individual confidentiality. Rates are calculated by dividing the number of cases by the population size for a specified time period. When comparing rates between populations, standardization of the denominator is necessary for direct comparisons. Factors influencing the interpretation of case-reporting data include population size changes, increases in HIV testing coverage, adoption of new case definitions, changes in treatment guidelines, and reporting practices. Surveillance data are typically presented using figures, tables, and maps, with clear titles, footnotes, and definitions of abbreviations.
